content: The Facilitation Manual: Psychological First Aid during Ebola Disease Outbreaks is a comprehensive guide designed to train helpers in providing psychological first aid (PFA) to individuals affected by Ebola outbreaks. PFA is a humane, supportive, and practical approach to assisting distressed individuals while respecting their dignity, culture, and abilities. This manual is intended to be used alongside the guide Psychological First Aid during Ebola Virus Disease Outbreaks (WHO, CBM, World Vision International, UNICEF, September 2014). The manual is divided into three main sections: 1. Overview of the Manual: This section provides general information on how to use the manual, prepare for delivering an orientation, and tips for facilitators. 2. Step-by-Step Orientation: This section outlines a full-day orientation agenda and provides detailed descriptions of each module. It includes learning objectives, facilitator narratives and tips, accompanying slides, and instructions for group exercises and discussions. 3. Supporting Materials: This section contains annexes with materials that can be printed as handouts for participants. How to Use the Manual The manual is designed for a full-day orientation (approximately five and a half hours, excluding breaks) to prepare helpers to support individuals recently affected by an Ebola outbreak. It is essential to adapt the orientation and materials to the local culture, language, and context, as well as to the specific needs of the participants. If a translator is used, they should be familiar with PFA and the orientation materials beforehand. Facilitators are encouraged to bring their own style, experience, and ideas to the orientation. Learning Objectives for Participants The orientation aims to build the capacity of helpers in crisis situations by teaching them: How to approach a situation safely for themselves and others. How to provide supportive and appropriate assistance to distressed individuals. How to avoid causing further harm through their actions. Participants will have opportunities to develop and practice PFA skills, but the orientation does not provide clinical counseling skills. A key objective is to help participants understand the boundaries of the support they can provide and when to refer individuals for specialized assistance. Helpers must also be aware of safety precautions and how to refer individuals with Ebola symptoms for medical care. Target Audience for the Manual Facilitators using this manual often have experience in mental health and psychosocial support. It is helpful if they also have: Prior experience assisting individuals affected by crisis events. Knowledge of Ebola virus disease and safety precautions. Interest and experience in providing orientation and training. The manual is suitable for both professionals and non-professionals who are in a position to help individuals affected by distressing events, such as an Ebola outbreak. This includes staff or volunteers from disaster relief organizations, health workers, teachers, community members, local government officials, and others. Helpers do not need a background in psychosocial or mental health to offer PFA. Participants should ideally have the time and willingness to assist in an Ebola outbreak situation, be accessible and available to help distressed individuals, and be connected with a recognized agency or group for safety and coordination. Preparing to Deliver the Orientation Before delivering a PFA orientation, facilitators should: Check with local authorities and obtain permission for the gathering if needed. Take time to prepare for the orientation to ensure it runs smoothly and is a valuable experience for participants. Preparation involves: Familiarizing oneself with the PFA guide, this manual, and the background of participants (e.g., culture, language, profession, helping role). Understanding Ebola disease, its transmission, and prevention. Reviewing key documents, such as the Inter-Agency Standing Committee Guidelines on Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in Emergencies. Facilitators should also prepare materials and handouts, such as printed copies of the two-page pocket guide or the full guide. Translating the pocket guide into the local language, if possible, can be helpful. Orientation materials should be tailored to the cultural and social context of participants, including adapting or creating new case scenarios based on the local context and the roles of participants. Preparing the Venue The choice of venue depends on the situation. In acute crisis situations, proper meeting rooms and facilities may not be available, so alternative spaces like tents or outdoor areas can be used. Facilitators should ensure the venue is adequate and ready by checking for: Sufficient space for the number of participants. Comfort and safety for participants. Privacy and quiet (if relevant, check the venue’s sound system beforehand). Tables and chairs that can be moved or arranged flexibly for role play and group work. Necessary equipment, such as a laptop, LCD projector, flipchart, whiteboard, markers, pens, notebooks, and refreshments. Facilitation Tips Facilitators can enhance the learning environment by: 1. Modeling the Skills: Demonstrate the skills and qualities you want participants to learn, such as being friendly, warm, relaxed, and calm. Use good verbal and non-verbal communication skills to convey interest and enthusiasm. Show positive regard, respect, and non-judgment. 2. Creating a Safe and Supportive Atmosphere: Set ground rules at the start of the orientation to maintain a productive and supportive environment. Acknowledge that the orientation may touch on distressing stories or personal experiences. Be available to assist participants who appear distressed or come to you with concerns. Listen without judgment and help them feel calm. 3. Utilizing Participatory Learning: Use participatory methods like simulations, role plays, and case scenarios to help participants develop PFA skills. These methods allow participants to practice their skills in a safe environment, receive feedback, and learn from each other. Encourage participants to adapt PFA to the local context. 4. Managing Time Well: Limit lecture time and engage participants in exchanging ideas and experiences through dialogue. Acknowledge participants’ existing knowledge and natural helping abilities. Be encouraging and positive as participants practice new skills. Invite questions and allow time for clarification. Be open to feedback and make adjustments as needed. Encouraging Participation Facilitators can encourage participation by: Starting with introductions so participants can meet each other. Learning and using participants’ names (name tags are helpful). Asking participants about their expectations for the orientation. Using energizers (games) to engage participants. Acknowledging that it takes courage to try role plays and that both successes and mistakes are valuable for learning. By following these guidelines, facilitators can create an effective and supportive learning environment for participants to develop the skills needed to provide psychological first aid during Ebola disease outbreaks.
